exercises.title: Replacing 'the data is bad' with the real data quality dimensions
exercises.situation: A business stakeholder says 'the customer data is just bad' and wants to know, in plain terms, what's actually wrong with it before the team spends budget fixing it.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd tell them the data has a lot of errors and missing stuff, so we should clean it up.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: 'Errors and missing stuff' doesn't say which quality dimension is actually broken, points to no evidence, and gives the stakeholder nothing to prioritize against — cleanup effort could target the wrong tables entirely.
exercises.professionalResponse: Rather than call it 'bad,' I'd break it into the specific data quality dimensions and show which ones are actually failing. I'd run profiling with SQL against the customer table first — null rates, distinct counts, pattern checks — to get real numbers instead of impressions. If 12% of phone numbers are null, that's a completeness problem; if state codes don't match a valid list, that's validity; if the same customer has two different addresses in CRM and billing, that's consistency; if duplicate account IDs show up for one person, that's uniqueness; if addresses haven't been refreshed in three years, that's timeliness. I'd map each finding to a dimension, prioritize by which critical data elements it touches — customer identity and billing address matter more than a rarely-used middle-name field — and present it as a scorecard so the business can see exactly where quality sits today and track whether remediation actually moves the number.

vocabulary.definition: The named categories — accuracy, completeness, consistency, validity, uniqueness, timeliness — used to describe specifically what kind of problem a dataset has.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Naming the dimension turns a vague complaint into a specific, fixable problem.

vocabulary.definition: Systematically examining a dataset's actual values — null rates, distinct counts, patterns — to understand its real condition.

vocabulary.definition: The data quality dimension measuring whether required values are present rather than missing.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: A high null rate on a required field like phone number is a completeness failure, not a vague 'error.'
vocabulary.example: If 12% of phone numbers are null, that's a completeness problem specifically.

vocabulary.definition: The data quality dimension measuring whether a value actually conforms to its expected format, type, or allowed list.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: A state code that isn't on the real list of valid states is a validity failure even if the field isn't blank.
vocabulary.example: State codes that don't match a valid list point to a validity issue, not a missing-data issue.

vocabulary.definition: A data field identified as high-priority because of its business, regulatory, or financial importance.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It lets you prioritize fixing customer identity before a rarely-used field, instead of treating every error equally.
vocabulary.example: I'd prioritize remediation by which critical data elements the findings actually touch.

vocabulary.definition: A summary report showing measured quality scores per dimension and per dataset, tracked over time.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It gives stakeholders a way to see the baseline and verify whether remediation actually worked.
vocabulary.example: I'd present it as a scorecard so the business can track whether remediation moves the number.

vocabulary.definition: A monitoring technique that tracks a metric's natural variation over time with calculated upper and lower control limits, distinguishing a genuine shift from normal noise.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's a more rigorous way to watch a quality metric than a single scorecard snapshot — it tells you whether a drop is a real trend or expected variation. This course's scorecard lesson covers presenting a point-in-time score; control charts go a step further into statistical monitoring, which is enrichment territory here.
vocabulary.example: Rather than reacting to one bad week, I'd want a control chart to confirm this drop is outside normal variation before escalating it.

exercises.title: Untangling 'the data dictionary thing' into glossary, dictionary, and catalog
exercises.situation: A new business analyst keeps calling the business glossary, the data dictionary, and the data catalog all 'the data dictionary thing' and asks you to explain the difference so they know where to look for what.
exercises.beginnerResponse: They're all basically the same place where you can look up what a field means.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It treats three distinct governance artifacts as interchangeable, gives the analyst no way to know which tool actually answers which question, and says nothing about who maintains each one or how they connect.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd separate the three deliberately, because they answer different questions. The business glossary holds business-friendly definitions of business concepts — what 'Active Customer' means to the company — governed by stewards through a glossary governance and approval workflow. The data dictionary documents the actual physical structures: real tables, real columns, real data types, tied to the technical implementation. The data catalog is the searchable inventory that sits across both — it links business and technical metadata together and surfaces ownership and lineage, so you can search 'Active Customer' and find both the glossary definition and the exact CustomerStatus column in the warehouse that implements it. I'd walk through a concrete example: 'Active Customer' is defined once in the glossary, that definition maps to the CustomerStatus column documented in the data dictionary, and both are discoverable together when you search the catalog — so the analyst knows to go to the glossary for meaning, the dictionary for structure, and the catalog when they don't know which table to start from at all.

exercises.title: Explaining who's actually accountable: owner, steward, custodian, consumer
exercises.situation: A manager asks 'who owns this data' after a dispute over who should approve a change to a shared customer table, and wants the roles explained clearly.
exercises.beginnerResponse: IT owns it since they run the database.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It conflates technical custody of the database with business accountability for the data's meaning and quality, and ignores that governance deliberately separates these roles — it gives no path to actually resolving the approval dispute.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd separate accountability from execution from custody from use. The data owner is the business-accountable party — for customer data, that's typically a business leader like the VP of Sales — who's accountable for the data's meaning, quality standards, and approving significant changes. The data steward is the named person who handles day-to-day definitions, quality rules, and stewardship on the owner's behalf. The data custodian is IT or the DBA team who physically stores, secures, and administers the database, but doesn't decide what the data should mean or whether a change is appropriate. The data consumers are everyone downstream building reports off it. I'd use a RACI breakdown to resolve the actual dispute: the owner is Accountable for approving the change, the steward is Responsible for assessing its impact and documenting it, the custodian is Consulted on technical feasibility and security constraints, and consumers are Informed once it's decided. So the change should route through the owner's approval, get executed by the custodian, and get documented by the steward — not get decided by whoever happens to run the server.

exercises.title: Naming the actual classification instead of just saying 'sensitive'
exercises.situation: A colleague says a new marketing table 'probably has some sensitive stuff in it' and asks you to just restrict access broadly. Explain how you'd actually classify it instead of locking the whole table down.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'll just mark the whole table as private so nobody except admins can see it.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It restricts everything without identifying what's actually sensitive, blocks legitimate business use of the non-sensitive columns, skips any real classification scheme, and isn't scalable or auditable as a decision.
exercises.professionalResponse: Rather than lock down the whole table, I'd identify specifically what's sensitive first. I'd run discovery over the table to find which columns actually contain PII — name, email, phone — versus merely confidential business data like a campaign budget, versus genuinely public information. I'd apply a real classification scheme with defined labels, like Public, Internal, Confidential, and Highly Confidential, rather than a binary private/not-private flag, and apply a sensitivity label at the column level where the actual PII lives. Then I'd apply column-level masking or row-level security only on those specific sensitive columns, so marketing analysts can still query campaign performance without seeing raw customer PII. I'd document the classification decision through the classification governance process so it's consistent with how other PII is handled elsewhere, not a one-off judgment call. Before closing it out, I'd validate the restriction actually works by checking, as a non-privileged user, which columns are visible and which are masked.

exercises.title: Why the CRM and the warehouse disagree on customer count
exercises.situation: Finance reports 42,000 active customers from the CRM while the data warehouse dashboard shows 39,500. Explain how you'd investigate the discrepancy.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just recount both and see which number is right.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: 'Recounting' isn't an investigation method — it doesn't check whether the two systems are even measuring the same definition of 'active,' doesn't use SQL to reconcile the actual records, and gives no way to prevent this from recurring next month.
exercises.professionalResponse: Before touching any numbers, I'd confirm both systems are counting the same definition of 'active customer' — I'd check the business glossary for the authoritative definition, since a mismatch here would explain the whole gap without any data being wrong at all. Assuming the definition is consistent, I'd run a cross-system reconciliation check in SQL: join on customer ID between the CRM extract and the warehouse table, and bucket results into matched, CRM-only, and warehouse-only. I'd profile the CRM-only set specifically — this is usually either a filter difference, like the warehouse excluding trial accounts that CRM still counts, or an ETL timing lag. I'd also run a referential integrity check for orphaned warehouse rows tied to customers already deleted in CRM. Once I isolate the actual cause — say, the ETL filter silently drops 'pending' status customers that CRM still counts as active — I'd fix whichever side is actually wrong, the filter or the glossary definition, and re-run the reconciliation check to confirm the counts now match. I'd close by setting this reconciliation check to run automatically on a schedule so this surfaces as a monitored alert next time, not a surprise finance notices first.

exercises.title: Duplicate customer records are breaking billing and mailings
exercises.situation: Customer service reports that the same customer is getting two separate invoices and two pieces of direct mail, suggesting duplicate master records. Explain how you'd investigate and fix it.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just search for customers with the same name and delete the extra one.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: Name-matching alone produces false positives and false negatives — nicknames, typos, and different people sharing a name all break it — and 'delete' destroys transaction history attached to whichever record gets removed, with no review step to catch a wrong merge.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd treat this as a data matching problem, not a simple duplicate-name search. I'd run matching using both deterministic rules, like an exact match on a reliable key such as email plus phone, and probabilistic matching, which fuzzy-matches name and address with a confidence score, to catch near-duplicates deterministic rules would miss, like 'Jon Smith' versus 'Jonathan Smith' at the same address. Matches above a high confidence threshold get flagged for automatic merge; borderline matches route to match review and stewardship so a human steward confirms them, since an automatic wrong merge causes more damage than a slightly slower manual one. For confirmed duplicates, I'd apply survivorship rules — the most recent address wins, but the original account-open date and full transaction history are preserved — to build a single golden record, rather than deleting either side outright. I'd validate the fix by confirming billing and mailing now pull from the golden record and that the merged transaction history from both original records is intact and complete.

exercises.title: Choosing between centralized, federated, and decentralized governance
exercises.situation: Leadership at a company with five semi-autonomous regional business units asks you to recommend a governance operating model. Explain your reasoning and recommendation.
exercises.beginnerResponse: We should just have one central team handle all governance for everyone.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It ignores the real tradeoffs — a single centralized team is often slow and disconnected from local nuance in a multi-business-unit organization — and names no alternative or criteria for choosing between models.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd walk through the three real operating models and their tradeoffs before recommending one. Centralized governance puts one team in charge of all policy and execution — strong consistency, but slow and disconnected from each region's local nuance. Decentralized governance lets each business unit govern independently — fast and locally accurate, but produces inconsistent standards and duplicated effort across five units. Federated governance splits the difference: a central team sets enterprise-wide policy, naming standards, and shared tooling like the catalog and classification scheme, while each business unit's own stewards handle day-to-day stewardship within that framework, escalating conflicts to a cross-unit governance council. Given five semi-autonomous business units, each with its own local context, I'd recommend federated: central policy and shared infrastructure, local execution. I'd validate the model is actually working by tracking two things over time — local steward engagement staying high, since that's what collapses under an overly centralized model, and enterprise-wide metrics like glossary consistency and classification coverage staying uniform across units, since that's what collapses under an overly decentralized one.

exercises.title: Weighing data mesh against a single centralized catalog for a multi-domain company
exercises.situation: A company with distinct finance, supply chain, and customer domains, each generating its own data products, asks whether to adopt a data mesh approach or stick with one centralized governance team and catalog. Explain the tradeoffs.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Data mesh is the newer approach so we should just switch to that.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It picks an architecture by trend rather than organizational fit, and ignores that data mesh shifts real governance responsibility onto domain teams who may not have the maturity or tooling to carry it yet.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd compare these on actual tradeoffs, not trendiness. A centralized catalog architecture concentrates metadata, lineage, and quality ownership in one team — consistent and easier to govern early on, but it becomes a bottleneck as domains scale and the central team loses context on data it doesn't own day-to-day. Data mesh governance treats each domain's data as an owned product with its own glossary terms, quality SLAs, and stewardship, operating under federated computational governance — shared platform-level policy enforcement for things like access and classification, with domain-level autonomy over the data itself. The real question isn't which approach is newer, it's organizational readiness: does finance, supply chain, and customer each have the maturity, per the governance maturity model, to genuinely own a data product with real SLAs, or would decentralizing governance just scatter accountability without the platform tooling in place to enforce consistency. For this company, I'd recommend starting with federated governance — a shared Purview catalog and classification standard centrally, domain ownership of glossary terms and quality rules locally — as a maturity step toward full data mesh, rather than jumping straight there, and I'd validate readiness with a single-domain pilot before rolling the model out further.

exercises.title: Designing the Unity Catalog structure for a shared Databricks lakehouse
exercises.situation: Three analytics teams are about to share one Databricks workspace, and leadership wants a governance structure that keeps each team's data isolated by default while still allowing approved cross-team sharing. Explain your design.
exercises.beginnerResponse: We'll just give everyone admin access to the workspace so nobody gets blocked.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It defeats the entire purpose of isolation, ignores least privilege, and produces an unauditable setup where nobody's access is actually scoped to their own team's data.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd design this around Unity Catalog's actual object hierarchy rather than solving access problems with blanket admin rights. One metastore serves the whole workspace, with a separate catalog per team, so isolation happens structurally at the top of the hierarchy, not by convention or trust. Within each catalog, schemas separate raw, curated, and reporting layers. Principals are modeled as Entra ID groups per team rather than individual grants, with privileges issued via GRANT at the catalog or schema level so permission management actually scales as the teams grow. Ownership of each catalog goes to that team's lead, who can delegate further access without routing every request through central IT, and inheritance of permissions means a grant at the catalog level flows down to its schemas and tables automatically, cutting down on repetitive manual grants. For the approved cross-team sharing requirement, rather than opening a whole catalog to another team, I'd use row filters and column masks on a specifically shared view, or Delta Sharing if the sharing needs to extend to a separate workspace entirely, keeping the underlying tables isolated either way. I'd validate this design by having an analyst from one team attempt to query another team's catalog directly and confirming it's denied, then confirming the explicitly shared view works exactly as intended.

exercises.situation: After an acquisition, the company now has its primary data estate in Azure and the acquired company's data in AWS S3 and Glue, and leadership wants one consistent governance approach rather than two separate ones. Explain how you'd architect this.
exercises.beginnerResponse: We should just migrate everything from AWS to Azure so it's all one system.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It defaults to an expensive, risky, full-scale migration as the first answer without considering governance-layer solutions that don't require moving the data at all, and ignores the timeline and business disruption a migration like that would cause.
exercises.professionalResponse: Before recommending anything as disruptive as migration, I'd architect governance across both clouds as they actually stand today, since migration is a separate, much larger decision with its own cost-benefit case. I'd apply the shared responsibility model for data to clarify what each cloud provider secures versus what the governance team has to handle itself in both environments. For identity, I'd federate access through Microsoft Entra ID as the single identity plane, mapped to Azure RBAC on the Azure side and to AWS IAM roles via federation on the AWS side, so access reviews happen in one place instead of two separate processes. For cataloging, I'd extend Purview's data map to register and scan the AWS S3 and Glue Data Catalog sources alongside the existing Azure Data Lake Storage sources, giving one unified catalog and classification scheme across both clouds instead of maintaining Glue's catalog and Purview's catalog as two inconsistent, disconnected systems — that's cross-cloud cataloging and lineage, and it's the actual governance answer to 'one consistent approach' that doesn't require moving a single byte of data. I'd validate this by confirming a single classification label applied in Purview is discoverable and behaves consistently whether you search for an Azure-sourced or an AWS-sourced asset.

exercises.title: Making the business case for a governance program leadership doesn't think they need
exercises.situation: The CFO says data governance sounds like 'a lot of process for not much benefit' and wants a business case before approving budget and headcount. Explain how you'd make the case.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Governance is important so we should just get budget for it because every company needs it.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It asserts importance without evidence or numbers, doesn't speak the CFO's language of cost and ROI, and gives nothing concrete for the CFO to actually approve or reject.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd build the case from the cost of poor data that's already happening today, not a hypothetical future risk. I'd pull real numbers: hours finance spends monthly reconciling conflicting reports, a specific compliance exposure like being unable to answer a data subject request within the regulatory window, or a deal or audit that was delayed because nobody could confirm an authoritative source for a key figure. I'd translate those into dollar terms — analyst hours lost to firefighting, estimated regulatory exposure, delayed revenue recognition — and weigh that against the proposed program's actual cost: not a full org-wide rollout, but a scoped governance pilot targeting one high-impact domain, like customer or financial data. I'd propose starting with that pilot, with a defined timeline and a measurable KPI, such as cutting reconciliation time by a specific percentage or closing a named audit finding, rather than asking the CFO to approve an open-ended program. That way the CFO is approving a bounded, measurable bet instead of an abstract 'process,' and I'd commit to reporting back against those exact KPIs at a fixed checkpoint.

exercises.title: Presenting a data quality scorecard result that isn't good news
exercises.situation: The quarterly data quality scorecard shows the finance data domain dropped from 92% to 78% on completeness, and you need to present this to the data governance steering committee. Explain how you'd communicate it.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just show them the number dropped and say we need to fix it.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: A bare number drop with no cause, no business-impact framing, and no plan invites either panic or dismissal — it gives the committee nothing to actually decide on.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd present this scorecard drop with the root cause already attached, not as a raw alarming number. I'd explain what actually changed — a new source system went live mid-quarter without the same validation rules as the legacy system, so new records are landing with missing fields that trip the existing SQL data quality checks. I'd frame the business impact precisely: which specific reports or decisions rely on the affected critical data elements, and what's genuinely at risk if it isn't fixed, whether that's a compliance filing deadline or a board-level metric. I'd present the remediation plan with a timeline and an interim mitigation, like routing the new source through a cleansing step before it lands, and set a clear re-measurement date so the committee isn't just told 'we're working on it' with no checkpoint. I'd also use this as the moment to recommend extending data quality monitoring to catch this kind of regression the moment a new source goes live, rather than finding out a quarter later from the scorecard.

exercises.situation: During a classification sweep, you discover a reporting table used by several analysts contains unmasked customer Social Security numbers that were never flagged as sensitive. You need to report this to leadership. Explain how you'd communicate it.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just tell them there's a security problem with the customer table and we're fixing it.

exercises.professionalResponse: I'd report this with the precision the situation actually requires, not softened language. I'd state exactly what was found — unmasked Social Security numbers, a specific PII category, in a reporting table with analyst-level access, discovered through a classification sweep — and immediately flag that this needs a formal assessment against the relevant regulatory breach-notification triggers, since depending on actual access and jurisdiction this could qualify as a reportable incident. That's a legal and compliance determination, not something I'd decide unilaterally. I'd present the immediate containment steps already taken or proposed — restricting access to the table right now, and applying a sensitivity label with column-level masking going forward — clearly separated from the root-cause question of how this went unclassified in the first place, which points to a gap in the classification governance process, likely a new table that bypassed the sensitive-data discovery scan. I'd close with concrete next steps: a formal privacy impact assessment, and a review of why the classification sweep didn't catch this table sooner so a similar gap doesn't exist elsewhere right now.

exercises.title: Proving a new data quality rule actually catches what it's supposed to
exercises.situation: You've written a new SQL data quality check meant to catch invalid email addresses before they load into the warehouse, and your manager asks how you know it actually works before it goes into production. Explain how you'd validate it.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I ran it against the table and it flagged some bad emails, so it works.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: 'Flagged some bad emails' isn't validation — it doesn't test for false negatives it might be missing, false positives it might be wrongly flagging, edge cases, or a tolerance threshold, so there's no actual evidence the rule is reliable.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd validate this the way a quality rule should actually be tested, not just run once and eyeballed. I'd build a deliberate test set: known-good emails, known-bad emails like missing @ symbols or bad domains, and edge cases that are valid but unusual, like plus-addressing or international domains. I'd run the rule against that set and check both directions — did it catch every known-bad case, which is recall, and did it wrongly flag any known-good case, which is the false-positive rate. A rule with a high false-positive rate causes just as much damage as one that misses real problems, since valid customer records get rejected or quarantined unnecessarily. I'd also set an explicit threshold and tolerance for the rule's failure rate, like alerting if more than 2% of a daily load fails this check, rather than treating every single failure as equally urgent — a brand-new source system genuinely having 1% malformed emails might be expected, while a sudden jump to 15% signals a real upstream break. Before production, I'd run it against a recent full day of real historical data, not a hand-picked sample, confirm the failure rate matches what we'd expect from known data issues, and only then automate it to run on every load with monitoring attached.

exercises.title: Proving a Snowflake role hierarchy actually enforces least privilege
exercises.situation: You've designed a Snowflake role hierarchy so that analysts can query masked customer data but not the underlying unmasked columns, and your manager asks how you'd confirm this actually holds up before go-live. Explain how you'd validate it.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I created the roles and granted the right privileges, so it should work as designed.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: Grants can propagate through the role hierarchy in unintended ways, and masking policies can be silently bypassed through indirect paths like a new view or a different warehouse context — none of that is visible just from reading the GRANT statements themselves.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd validate this by actually logging in as a representative analyst role and running real queries, not just reviewing the grants. First I'd confirm the masking policy is attached correctly and that querying the base table as the analyst role actually returns masked values, not the raw column, since dynamic data masking policies can silently fail to apply if attached to the wrong object or if the role inherits through an unexpected path in the role hierarchy. I'd specifically test role hierarchy inheritance: does the analyst role, through any parent role, pick up a broader privilege than intended? I'd also check for bypass paths — can the analyst create their own view on top of the base table that exposes the unmasked column, or query through a different warehouse or role context the masking policy doesn't cover — since RBAC in Snowflake is enforced per-role, not per-person, and excess privilege anywhere in the chain breaks the whole design. Before go-live I'd also check access history to confirm no one has already queried the unmasked data during testing, and only sign off once a real analyst account, not an admin account, confirms they see exactly the masked view and nothing more.

exercises.situation: A regulatory audit is coming up and auditors will trace a sample of reported figures back to source to confirm lineage documentation is accurate. Your manager asks how confident you are in the lineage documentation, and you need to validate it before the audit rather than find out live. Explain how you'd do this.

exercises.professionalResponse: I'd treat this as a dry run of the audit itself rather than trusting the documentation is current. I'd pick a sample of reported figures the same way an auditor would, ideally the highest-risk or highest-value ones, and manually trace each one through the documented lineage: source system, through the ETL or ELT transformation and business rules, into the warehouse, through the semantic model, to the final report — confirming at each hop that what Purview's automated lineage shows actually matches the real current pipeline, not a snapshot from six months ago. I'd pay particular attention to any manual or semi-automated steps, since that's exactly the gap area — automated capture tools reliably track pipeline-to-pipeline lineage but often miss a manual Excel adjustment or an ad hoc SQL script someone ran once and forgot to document. Anywhere the trace breaks or the documentation doesn't match reality, I'd fix the lineage documentation and the underlying process gap that let it go stale, before the audit, not during it. I'd close by running the full lineage review checklist against the sampled figures and confirming the trace works end-to-end with no manual 'trust me' steps left undocumented.

exercises.title: Confirming an AI model's governance controls actually work before production
exercises.situation: A new customer-churn prediction model has a model card, passed its approval workflow, and is scheduled to go live next week. Your manager asks how you'd confirm the governance controls around it actually work, not just that the paperwork is complete. Explain how you'd validate it.
exercises.beginnerResponse: The model card is filled out and it got approved, so the governance side is done.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It treats documentation and a sign-off as proof the control actually works, when the real test is whether monitoring, access control, and drift detection function once the model is live — none of which a model card by itself proves.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd treat the paperwork as necessary but not sufficient, and validate that the operational controls actually function. First I'd confirm the model is actually registered in the model inventory and registry with current version metadata, not just that a document exists somewhere, so that if an incident happens next month, this model is traceable, not missing from the inventory. Then I'd test monitoring models in production before go-live, not after — deliberately feeding it a batch of data with a known distribution shift and confirming drift and performance monitoring actually fires an alert, rather than assuming the dashboard is wired up correctly. I'd verify access to models and data by confirming only the roles the approval workflow actually authorized can query or retrain this model, tested the same way I'd test any access control: by attempting access as an unauthorized role and confirming it's denied. I'd also confirm AI lineage is intact — can we trace this model's current version back to the exact training data snapshot and governance approval it was tied to, so a future audit doesn't hit a dead end. Only once monitoring, access control, and lineage are all confirmed working live, not just documented, would I sign off that the governance controls, not just the paperwork, are actually production-ready.
